items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: The group was intact with Buddy and Jim Hall, and Carson.

ctx.x: That sound with the cello and pianoless. Did that come about from sitting down and thinking let’s find something different here? Or was it a more practical—

Originally the group was going to be French horn, John Graas, he was the number one French horn player on the West Coast at that time when I formed the group. The group was intact with Buddy and Jim Hall, and Carson. And Buddy and I came up musically together. Cars and I were with Gerry together, and Jim Hall was just a stroke of luck. He needed a gig and he heard that I was organizing, putting a group together. Because he was stacking music in a music store at that time. He wasn’t even playing. And the day of…
And even had the part where the stick fell.

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I got myself together and got started with Jim Hall. ... And what about Jim Hall, because that was your founding group. Yeah. Jim lasted, you know, to the point -- Jim might have just got bored.

ctx.x: Did you learn anything about arranging and composition from him?

From he and Lenny both. They were both musical geniuses. Luther did a lot of stuff for Duke, which Duke took the credit for. Duke was (unintelligible), but anyway he was good. As a matter of fact I just -- Jim Hall’s daughter, Devra, she’s going to interview me on Wednesday and she’s doing a book on Luther. Do you know Devra?
No, but I knew Luther. I interviewed Luther for the Oral History.

items.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So that’s how I hooked up with Chico... Let’s talk a little bit about that quintet... there’s a picture of me with that on a Chico Hamilton Quintet CD.

ctx.x: So he had this piece he was working on, and he wanted me to look at it ‘cause he knew I had a background. So, it was a… oh, something about these guys were searching

for gold in the mountains of Mexico or something like that. And it’s two men went walking, searching for gold, and when they started… So, and then, so that was okay. He showed me that. And then the next, and when they started, he had six notes there, and I was trying to be polite. I said, “Senor Gomez, I think you have an extra note.” He says, “And when they es-started.” And then he said, “Oh.” (laughs) He changed it. So he was great. But… I can’t remember if I was working, starting to work with… In any case, I…

items.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Chico and me, I guess that’s it. The quintet. So it was a perfect job for me and we played at this club in Long Beach

ctx.x: I would really just like to know what your experience was with that. Did it click right away? Was it…? How, how did it [go?]?

Yeah, it was… Well, first of all, it literally was… I won’t say a lifesaver but I needed a job. (laughs) And I could, with my background I could, it would… Fred Katz played cello and piano. And then Buddy Collette played the woodwinds — clarinet and alto, and I don’t know if he played tenor. Carson Smith was the bass player, and Chico and me, I guess that’s it. The quintet. So it was a perfect job for me and we played at this club in Long Beach — The Strollers — for months. So I could write for the group and I…
We stick to the Chico group just for a minute.
